I do not propose, in making this brief review of the material contained in this volume XVIII of the translation of the Works of Saint Augustine, to present a study of all the matters it deals with or of any of them, which is rather work that requires another occasion; Therefore, here I will point out the circumstance and time of its appearance and the subject matter it deals with, highlighting its most main points, so that the reader becomes interested in reading its content in the original, since this is the main purpose attempted with the translation of these works. The book that Augustine writes about the exposition of some propositions or passages of the Epistle to the Romans was composed more occasionally than on his own. Well, being in Carthage in the year 394, while he was still a priest, as this Epistle of Saint Paul was read among the brothers who were gathered there, as he tells us in the first book of his Retractations (c.23), he was questioned, as it was being read, about some When answering the questions that the brothers asked him, they wanted to record in writing what he was answering orally. In this way the book was composed, which, as we can see from its reading, is not a comprehensive and detailed exposition of the recorded passages, since time and circumstances prevented it. Perhaps he had already conceived the idea of exposing this entire Epistle, verse by verse, as he attempted that same year, although he later did not carry it out. carried out, and that is why he does not go into details in most of the propositions; however, the problems he touches on in passing are of utmost importance in the dogmatic and moral question. The capital thought of the Epistle of Saint Paul is the grace and the works of the law. The converted Jews attributed the reception of the grace of the Gospel to the merits of the works of the law, and they considered the Gentiles as upstarts. deicides. Knowing this, Saint Paul goes out to meet them both, and explains the value of the law and what justification is due, demonstrating to some and others that they have no reason to boast or blame themselves, S. So that at first glance it does not appear that the Apostle disapproved of the law and that free will disappeared from man, Augustine says that four degrees must be considered in man: before the law, under the law, under grace and in rest. He has conceived the entire doctrine of the Epistle under these four degrees. Studying one by one, he concisely but masterfully explains how man finds himself in them, what value the law has, how grace works and how free will remains before grace. Incidentally, he deals with other points depending on the passage he comments on; Thus he makes us see in what admirable way the effect of grace surpasses that of sin, and exposes how the law makes sin evident, but does not erase it; here he puts the finishing touch to the "crede fortiter" of the Protestants; He also teaches what "the enmity with God of the prudence of the flesh" is so as not to fall into the error of the double Manichean principle. It makes us see what the spirit of slavery and adoption of which Saint Paul speaks consists of, to whom it applies and how. Dealing with the vocation of God, he explains how God carries it out, although he gives value to the "initium fidei" as something proper to man, for which he deserves this vocation or calling; but later, when he has studied the question of grace more thoroughly, as he says in the Retractions, he corrects this sentence and confesses that the same "initium fidei" is the grace of God. He also points out the difference in the names of Only Begotten and Firstborn that are given to the Lord. Of charity, the virtue by which the soul is united to God, he shows that only sin can take it away from us. Finally, it tells us about the behavior that Christians must observe among themselves and the obedience they must pay to civil powers. The reason that Saint Paul had for writing his Epistle to the Galatians was that certain Jews converted to Christianity had disturbed the church of Galatia, stating that to be saved, circumcision was necessary along with baptism, and, therefore, they wanted to force the Galatians to be circumcised and to fulfill the works of the law.

Saint Paul, after proving his mission in this Epistle and the conformity of his gospel with that of the other apostles, seriously rebukes the propagators of such doctrines and the Galatians themselves who were inclined to circumcision, and tells them strictly that no one is justified by the works of the law and that justification is carried out by living faith in Jesus Christ. They are the ones who execute them, and, finally, he makes an admirable study of fraternal correction. Augustine began his exposition of the Epistle of Saint Paul to the Romans around the year 394, after having finished his exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians. If he had finished the exposition of this Epistle, we would have had, as he tells us in the Retractions, a large number of books, given the length he gave to the exposition of the greeting of the letter, since he composed only one book from it and the incidental question of the sin against the Holy Spirit. Terrified, he says, by the excessiveness of the work and the undertaking of the work, he did not continue with his first attempt, and thus only left us a single book, which he titled Inchoate Exposition of the Epistle to the Romans. Truly, when reading this book one is amazed at the exposition it makes of each word of the Apostle's greeting. Upon unraveling it, he observes how, without being named with proper names, the Trinity is expressed in him, the same as in the greetings of almost all the other epistles of him and the other apostles. He exposes in an admirable way how God's justice is combined with his mercy giving grace, and, taking as a starting point, he dedicates half of the book to the study of what the sin is against the Holy Spirit; To do this, he presents several kinds of sins, which at first glance seem to be those of which Jesus Christ said in the Gospel: "Whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this world nor in the next." After studying each one by itself and seeing how they are all forgiven, he concludes that the sin against the Holy Spirit, which the Lord said is not forgiven neither in this world nor in the next, consists of final impenitence or permanence until the last moment of life in iniquity and evil, despairing of God's forgiveness; understanding what Jesus Christ says: "Whoever speaks a word", not only as a voice, but also as an action or work. In the First Letter of Saint J'iian, titled, according to Saint Augustine and other writers, To the Parthians, the divinity of the Word and humanity, passion and death in Jesus Christ are defended. The main point is established for the good works of the Christian, since faith without works, charity, does not save; so that almost the entire Epistle revolves around this thought.

Saint Augustine was discussing the Gospel of Saint John with the faithful when he began the exposition of this Epistle, which he presented to the people in ten sermons. The circumstance was having to interrupt the Gospel of

Saint John because, according to custom, as he tells us in the prologue of the same exposition of the Epistle, during the days of Easter certain evangelical passages were read, and, by interrupting the order of the exposition of the Gospel of Saint John during those, he wanted, without departing from Saint John, to expound his first Epistle, thinking that it would have enough material for the Easter week, and above all attracted by the content of the Letter, since, like him He says, almost all of it deals with love, and there is nothing sweeter for all those who have a healthy palate of the heart, since this is the food of souls, bread of God who is God himself. This exhibition took place around the year 416. No wonder Christian devotion has presented Saint Augustine with a heart in his hand burned in flames of love. If anyone knew how to love God on earth, one of them was Augustine, as can be seen in all his works, and mainly in those where he expressly talks about love. Like another John, from whom he has learned that God is love, he transcends the things of earth and goes in search of the side of Christ, because he knows that love is contained there. That is why he comments on this Letter with extraordinary pleasure, highlighting charity so that it may be loved by men. In the first treatise or sermon that he addressed to the people about it, following Saint John step by step, he first presents Christ as the Word of life and, therefore, carrying out the deification of man, and he also tells us how he manifested himself to the angels and to man. If God is light and we must have union with God, we must cast darkness from us; But, since no one is without sin in this world, it is necessary that the blood of Christ erase him, confessing him and covering him with charity, which erases sins, because, if we do not have charity, if we do not love our brothers, we are in the darkness of sin and we continually stumble against Christ. In the second treatise he recommends the care that we must take to retain in memory the things that are read in Scripture regarding eternal health, so that we can oppose the enemies, and see clearly in doubts, so that what happens to the disciples of Emmaus does not happen to us. Then he addresses the heretics, mainly the Donatists, to demonstrate to them what the true Church is and how it is not found in the parts of Donatus.

Explaining the verses of Saint John in which he speaks to children, parents, young people and children, he tells us who erases sin, who is the Principle and how children and young people should behave. Finally, he exhorts us to hate the love of the world, showing how it is

the man in it, and how he finds himself in the middle of the current of an impetuous river carried by the three loves of the earth; But the Christ tree is planted on the shore so that he can grasp its branches and thus be free from death. In the third sermon he speaks to the children in faith, exhorting them to believe and to get closer, to achieve this, to the mother's breasts, which are the. two Testaments, so that, nourished by them, they may come to eat the strong delicacy, which is the Word of life. And so that no one is carried away by laziness, he tells them that they must take into account, as the apostle indicates, "that it is the last hour," in which the antichrists have appeared, from whose doctrine they must beware. It declares who the antichrists are, how they are known, how they left the Church not being of it, and how there are others in it who have not yet left; Their words should not be taken into account, since many times they confess Christ with their mouths, but deny Him with their actions. Finally, he points out the reward for which man must work, and who is the Teacher, who, having his chair in heaven, truly indoctrinates the interior of man, since the other teachers are like the farmer for the earth. Continuing in the fourth sermon with the Master of the interior, he points out who it is that wants to supplant him, and he exhorts us not to abandon him, because He is truthful and just, who makes us truthful and just through the love he professes for us. He then explains how he makes us righteous and how we must fight to achieve justice and thus become like God and be children of God. Here he admirably explains how far this similarity with God and being children of God goes, and ends the sermon by exposing how we become children of the devil through sin, which those who are born of God and remain in Him do not commit. The fifth sermon begins with the question originated by the two, apparently opposite, testimonies of the apostle Saint John: "He who is born of God does not sin," and "if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves."

He solves it by telling us that it is a sin against love for one's brothers, against the new mandate of Christ, against charity, since this alone is what distinguishes the children of God from the children of the devil, and it is the perfection of the law; and that is why it is not strange that the world hates the children of God, because it lacks charity. He concludes the sermon by pointing out how charity begins and is perfected in man.

The sixth sermon begins by saying that one should not love only in words and with the tongue, but with deeds and truth. To know who acts like this, resort to the testimony of conscience, looking and trusting in God and his commandment. Next, he studies the trust we must have in God, and how and in what way God always hears those who trust in Him and keep the commandment of love, even if it seems otherwise. Then he teaches to distinguish the spirit of God and the world, putting the distinction in the love of brothers. The seventh sermon begins by telling us how the children of God are on earth, having in it a fountain, which God placed so that we would not perish along the way: charity; and that those who disturb it deny Christ and are of the world. Us says that we must belong to God, and explains that we will only be so through charity. Then he exposes the testimony of Saint John, who says: "Charity comes from God, and God is charity"; and how God loved us so that we would love Him, ending the exposition of this passage rapt with love, saying: "Love, and do what you want"; love cannot do evil, it is God. To conclude the sermon he tells us that God is invisible, the same as charity; but, although it has no material forms, the pure in heart will see God; and that with the understanding he who has charity sees him; That is why he encourages it to be possessed and not remain inactive. The eighth sermon begins by saying that charity is sweet in its word, but it is sweeter in its work. After telling us that she can always be active and listing her works, she admonishes us not to seek our praise in them, because it would cease to be charity. He then explains why Saint John insists on the love of his brother, barely mentioning the love of God and almost completely keeping silent about the love of the enemy. Since sin is opposed to God and the root of all sin is greed, according to one passage of Scripture, and, according to another, the beginning of all sin is pride, it makes us see how greed is in pride; Study these two vices and indicate how pride dresses itself in the garb of charity to deceive us. He then teaches us to love our enemies, and ends the sermon by exhorting us to trust in Jesus Christ our Savior, who came to heal us; because, if we trust and confess that Jesus is the Son of God, God dwells in us and we in Him.

As the apostle says that we will have perfect charity if we have faith in the day of judgment, he explains what it means to have this faith, and, among other things, he tells us that one begins to believe in the day of judgment when one begins to fear; But he who fears does not yet have perfect charity, since "charity casts out fear." But, as it is said in another psalm that "chaste fear remains forever and ever," it seems to be opposed to what Saint John says. Study these two passages, and with some exquisite examples elucidate the issue, saying that both are true, because the one deals with penal fear, which is necessary so that charity can be introduced as a messenger and then disappear; The other is chaste fear, which is charity and endures forever and ever. Finally, we are excited to love God because He loved us first and deformed, and if we fulfill this, we also love our brothers, we love charity, because these loves are reciprocal, or rather, they are one. • Since faith is necessary for there to be charity, and charity and faith without works are of no use, this last sermon begins by telling us what faith should be like; faith in Christ that Saint John says, because He is the way, the truth and the life. He then explains how we believe in Christ, to know in this way if we love our neighbor, if we love God, if we love charity; and invites us to climb this mountain, Christ, which is the end of the law or the command. and the fullness of the commandment is charity, and charity is God, so that from there we may contemplate the expiration of the things of the world and the eternal permanence of charity. Finally, he exhorts us to fulfill the law, which is contained in the commandment of the love of God and neighbor, loving Christ, the Word of God, in his head and in his members; His head is in the heavens, his members lie on the earth. He ends by saying that, as children keep their father's last words in their hearts and fulfill them, so we must fulfill the last and new command of Christ: the commandment of love. F R. Therefore before the law we do not fight, because we not only ardently desire and sin, but we also approve of sins; Under the law we fight, but we are defeated; We confess, therefore, that the actions we do are bad, and, confessing that they are bad, we certainly do not want to do them; but, since grace is still lacking, we are defeated. In this degree we become aware of how prostrate we are, and as we try to get up and fall, we are more severely tormented. Hence it was said: the law was introduced so that crime would abound. Hence also what is now written: sin is known by the law; but it does not make sin disappear, because sin is erased only through grace. Therefore the law is good, since it prohibits the things that should be prohibited and commands the things that should be commanded. But, when someone judges that he must fulfill the law with his own strength and not with the grace of his Deliverer, this presumption does him no good; In fact, it harms so much that with greater desire he is attracted to sin and falls into sin. Because where there is no law there is no transgression. Finding himself fallen to the ground in this way, when someone would have known that he cannot help himself to get up, he implores the help of the Liberator. Then grace will come that forgives past sins, and helps those who try to emerge, and offers the charity of justice, and makes fear disappear. When this takes place, although some desires of the flesh oppose, while we are in this world, against our spirit to induce it to sin, nevertheless, since the spirit does not consent to such desires, since it is established in the grace and charity of God, it ceases to sin. We sin not by this evil desire, but by our consent. This is what the Apostle himself says: do not let sin reign in your mortal body to obey its own desires. By this he showed that there are desires to which, by not obeying, we do not allow sin to reign in us. But, since these desires are born from the mortality of the flesh, which we drag from the first sin of Adam, from whom we are carnally born, they will not end unless we deserve in the resurrection of the bodies that mortality that is promised to us, where there will be perfect peace, when we find ourselves established in that fourth degree. There will be perfect peace, because nothing opposes us when we do not oppose God. This is what the Apostle says: the body is certainly dead through sin, but the spirit is life through righteousness. Therefore, if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus Christ from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit, who dwells in you. Then the first man had perfect free will, but we before grace do not have free will not to sin, but only not to want to sin. But grace makes it so that we not only want to act with righteousness, but that we can, not by our own strength, but with the help of the Liberator, who will also give us perfect peace in the resurrection. This complete peace follows goodwill, because it is said: glory to God in the highest and peace on earth to men of good will.

I took charge of the exposition of the Epistle to the Romans, as I did with that written to the Galatians. But, if the exhibition of this work had finished, it would have taken up many books. Certainly the true doctrine of human justice consists in loving in oneself what is proper to God and in hating what is proper to man; in not approving one of his sins or reproving another in them outside of himself; in not judging that it is enough for someone to dislike his sins, without adding amendment in the future with careful vigilance; in not thinking that, without being helped by God, his own strength is sufficient to avoid sins. When the Apostle gives peace and grace on behalf of God the Father of the Lord our Jesus Christ, not to mention and on behalf of the Holy Spirit, it seems to me that he had no other motive than to give us to understand that the very gift of God is the Holy Spirit; For grace and peace, what else are they but the gift of God? Exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians

1. The reason for the apostle Saint Paul writing to the Galatians is so that they understand that the grace of God entails no longer being subject to the law. When the grace of the Gospel was preached to them, there were some of the circumcision who, although Christians, had not yet received the benefit of grace; Therefore, they still wanted to be subject to the burdens of the law, which the Lord God had imposed on the servants of sin, not on those of righteousness. He had given a just law to unjust men, to make their sins evident to them, but not to erase them, since nothing erases sins except the grace of faith, which works through love. Once the Galatians were already established under this grace, the Jews wanted to place them under the weight of the law, stating that the Gospel was of no use to them if they were not circumcised and submitted to the other carnal observances of the Jewish rite. For this reason, they began to suspect that the apostle Saint Paul, who had preached the Gospel to them, did not have the doctrine of the other apostles, who forced the Jews to be Judaized.

For it is easier to see what in another needs to be corrected, and to correct it by disapproving or reproaching, than to observe what needs to be corrected in yourself, and to correct it willingly yourself. How much less let yourself be corrected by another! How much less for an inferior! Much less in front of everyone! From here he begins to demonstrate how the grace of faith is sufficient to justify without the works of the law; lest anyone should say that he does not attribute all man's justification to the works of the law alone, nor to the grace of faith alone, but that health comes from both. But in order to deal with this question with all diligence, lest anyone be deceived by ambiguity, he must first know that the works of the law are divided into two parts. Some belong to the sacraments, some to customs. To the sacraments belong the circumcision of the flesh, the temporal Sabbath, the new moons, the sacrifices, and all innumerable similar observances. Customs include: you shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not bear false witness, and the like. Could the Apostle not worry about whether a Christian was a murderer, or an adulterer, or chaste, or innocent, just as he did not care if he was circumcised or had a foreskin? Now he deals in a special way with the works of the law that refer to the sacraments, although, however, he sometimes implies that he also mixes the others. Very close to the end considerent quo pretio emerit possessionem, quam in eis amittebat; ut parum esset gratis eum mortmim, quod superseis dixerat. Illud enim ita sonat, tanquam non pervenerit ad possessionem, pro qua sanguinem dedit. Proscribed autem etiam quae tenebat, auferuntur: sed haec proscriptio non obest Christo, qui etiam sic per divinitatem Dominus est omnium: sed ipsi possessioni, quae huius gratiae cultura caret. 19. Hinc iam incipit demonstrare quemadmodum gratia fidei sufficiat, ad iustificandum sine operibus Legis; ne quis diceret non se quidem operibus Legis tantum totam hominis iustificationem tribuere, sed ñeque tantum gratiae fidei, ex utroque autem perfici salutem. Sed haec quaestio ut diligenter tractetur, ne quis fallatur ambiguous, scire prius debent opera Legis bipartita esse. Nam partim in sacramentis, partim vero in moribus accipiuntur.

Ad sacramenta pertinent, circumcisio carnis, sabbatum temporale, neomeniae, sacrifice, atque omnes huiusmodi innumerae observationes. Ad mores autem, Non occides, Non moechaberis, Non jalsum testimonium dices", et talia caetera. Nunc ergo de his operibus maxime tractat, quae sunt in sacramentis, quanquam et illa interdum se admiscere significacet. Prope finem autem Epistolae, de his separatim tractabit, quae sunt in moribus: et illud breviter, hoc autem diutius.

of the epistle, he will deal separately with those that pertain to customs, dwelling little on them and much on these. All these observances, whose usefulness lies in understanding them, are presented to the Gentiles, because all of them are clarified to Christians so that they only understand what they are worth, but not to force them to execute them. These observances, if not understood, are only slavery, as the Jewish people had, and have to this day; If, on the contrary, they are fulfilled and understood, not only do they not harm, but they benefit if they adapt to time; just as they were observed by Moses and the prophets, fitting to that people, for whom such servitude was then useful in order to preserve themselves under fear. There is nothing that more piously overwhelms the soul than a sacrament not understood; On the contrary, if it is understood, it engenders a devout joy and is exalted without fear if there is time for it; If there is not, it is read and appreciated only with spiritual delight. Every sacrament, when understood, is applied to the contemplation of truth or good morals. The contemplation of truth is only founded on the love of God; good customs, in the love of God and neighbor, on whose two precepts the entire law and the prophets are based. Scriptures, too fearful of this sentence and defenders with due piety of the Old Testament, do not judge that this was said of the Lord, but rather of Judas the traitor; For they say that not everyone who is nailed to the tree was said to be cursed, but rather everyone who is hanged on a tree, because here it was not the Lord who was designated, but rather the one who hung himself on the noose. They ramble too much and do not pay attention to the fact that they litigate against the Apostle, who says: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, because it is written: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree. Therefore, he who became a curse for us is the same one who hung on the tree, that is, Christ, who freed us from the curse of the law so that from now on we would not justify ourselves by fear by the works of the law, but by faith before God, which works out of love and not out of fear. The Holy Spirit, who said this through Moses, took care of both things: that those who could not yet live by the faith of invisible things would be kept by the fear of visible punishments, and that He Himself made this fear disappear, taking what was feared, so that, once fear disappeared, He could give the gift of charity. It should not be considered an affront to the Lord to have called him cursed who hangs on the tree. Since, as to his mortal condition, he was hanged on the tree; and where mortality comes from is known to all believers, since it is derived from the penalty and curse of the sin of the first man, which the Lord took, bearing our sins in his body on the wood. If it were said that death was cursed, no one would be horrified; and what is

hung on the tree but only the death of the Lord to conquer death with death? Then the same one that was defeated was cursed. Likewise, if it were said: sin was cursed, no one would be surprised; And what was hung on the tree but the sin of the old man, which the Lord took for us in the mortality of the same flesh? Hence the Apostle did not blush, nor was he afraid to say that he became sin for us, adding: and because of sin he condemned sin. Our old man would not have been crucified at the same time, as the same Apostle says elsewhere, if the figure of our sin had not been hung in that death of the Lord so that the body of sin would be annulled so that from now on we would not be servants of sin. Representing this sin and death, Moses raised the serpent on the tree in the desert. By the persuasion of the serpent, man fell into the condemnation of death; therefore, the serpent was raised on a log congruently to represent death itself; In that figure the death of the Lord hung on the log. And who would be horrified if it were said: cursed is the snake that is hanging on the tree? And yet, the serpent, prefiguring the death of the Lord's flesh, hung from the tree, whose prefigurative mystery the Lord himself confirmed when he said: As Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so it is fitting that the Son of Man should be lifted up from the earth. She calls Jesus Christ Mediator inasmuch as he is a man, and this is most evident in that sentence of the Apostos himself, when he says: because there is one God and one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. There cannot be a mediator between God and God, because there is only one God, and the mediator does not belong to only one, because he is an intermediary between some. The angels, without a doubt, who did not depart from the vision of God, need no mediator by whom they may be reconciled. Likewise, the angels who, without anyone's incitement, departed from the vision of God through voluntary prevarication are not reconciled through a mediator. Then it remains for him who was brought down by the devil, a proud mediator who persuades pride, to rise up by Christ, a humble mediator of, who advises humility. Because, if the Son of God had wanted to remain in the natural equality of the Father and had not annihilated himself by taking the form of a servant, he would not be a mediator between God and men, because the Trinity is one God, the same in all three, in the Father, in the Son and in the Holy Spirit, for the eternity of the deity and for constant equality. to those who by nature are not gods, demonstrates with all evidence that the only true God is by nature God, under whose name the Trinity is understood in the most faithful and Catholic bosom of the heart. Those who are not by nature gods are called tutors and curators above, because there is no creature, whether that which abides in the truth giving glory to God, or that which did not abide in it, seeking its own glory, that by choice or by force does not serve divine Providence, since, willing, it does with it what is good, and of that which does not want to do good, it does what is just. Because, if the prevaricating angels themselves, with their prince the devil, were not rightly called tutors and curators of divine Providence, the Lord would not have called the devil magistrate of this world; Nor would the same apostolic authority have used it to correct men, as Saint Paul expresses it in another passage: I handed these over to Satan so that they would learn not to blaspheme. And in another place, referring to spiritual health, he says: for I, although absent with the body, but present with the spirit, have already condemned, as if I were present, the one who acted in this way. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, you and my spirit are gathered together, I have judged, by the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, to hand this one over to Satan for the perdition of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus Christ. But, as the magistrate who is constituted by the emperor does not act except what he allows, so the tutors and curators of this world execute nothing outside of what God tolerates them. Nothing is hidden from Him, as from men; nor does anything escape its power, so that the tutors and curators who are naturaliter non, sunt dii, servistis, satis demonstrat unum verum Deum natura esse Deum, quo nomine Trinitas fidelissimo et eatholico gremio cordis accipitur. Eos autem qui natura non sunt dii, propterea superius procuratores actorsque appellat, quia nulla creatura est, sive quae in veritate manet, dans gloriam Deo; sive quae in veritate non stetit, quaerens gloriam suam: nulla inquam creatura est, quae non, velit nolit, divinae providentiae serviat; sed volens facit cum ea quod bonum est; de illa vero quae hoc non vult, fit quod iustum est.

Christus ergo Verbum vitae. Et unde manifestata est? Erat enim ab initio; sed non erat manifestata hominibus: manifestata autem erat Angelis videntibus, et tanquam pane suo cibantibus. Sed quid ait Scriptura? Panem Angelorum manducavit homo 2. Ergo manifestata est ipsa vita in carne; quia in manifestatione posita est, ut res quae solo corde videri potest. videretur et oculis. ut corda sanaret. Solo enim corde videtur Verbum: caro autem et oculis corporalibus videtur. Erat unde videremus carnem. sed non erat unde videremus Verbum: factum est Verbum caro, quam videre possemus ut sanaretur in nobis unde Verbum videremus. 2. Et vidimus, the testes sumus. Forte aliqui fratrum nesciunt, qui graece non norunt, quid sint testes graece: et usitatum nomen est omnibus et religiosum; quos enim testes latine dicimus, graece martyres gunt. Quis autem non audivit martyres, aut in cuius christiani ore non quotidie habitat nomen martyrum? Atque utinam sic habitet et in corde, ut passiones martyrum imitemur, non eos calcibus persequamur! Ergo hoc dixit, Vidimus, et testes sumus: Vidimus, et martyres sumus. Testimonium enim dicendo ex eo quod viderunt, et testimonium dicendo ex eo quod audierunt ab his qui viderunt, cum displiceret ipsum testimonium hominibus adver-

They heard from the lips of the eyewitnesses, because their testimony displeased the men before whom they spoke, they endured all the sufferings that the martyrs endured. Witnesses of God are all the martyrs. God wanted to have men as witnesses, so that men would have God as witnesses. We saw, he says, and we are witnesses. Where did they see? At the demonstration. And what does it mean in the demonstration? In the sun, that is, in this light. How could He who made even the sun be seen in the sun, if it were not because He placed His prayer in the sun, and He, like a bridegroom coming out of the tabernacle, leaps like a giant to walk the path? He, who existed before the sun that made; He, who is before the star, before all the stars, before all the angels, true creator, because all things were made by Him, and without Him nothing was made, so that it could be seen by carnal eyes, which contemplate the sun, he placed his abode in the sun, that is, he let his flesh be seen in the manifestation of this light. The bedchamber of that husband was the womb of the Virgin, because in that virgin womb the two were united, the husband and the wife, that is, the Word and the flesh, since it is written: They will be two in one flesh. Also in the Gospel the Lord says: Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh. Isaiah excellently remembers that these two are one; Well, speaking of the person of Christ, he says: As a husband he imposed a miter on me and as a wife he adorned me with splendor. One only seems to be the one who speaks and becomes husband and wife, because they are not two, but one flesh, since the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. The Church is united to this flesh, and the complete body results: head and body. sus quos dicebatur, passi sunt omnia quae passi sunt martyres. Testes Dei sunt martyres. Deus testes habere voluit homines ut et nomines habeant testem Deum.

Vidimus, inquit, et testes sumus. Ubi viderunt? In manifestation. Quid est, in manifestatione? In solé, id est in hac luz. Unde autem potuit videri in sole qui fecit solem, nisi quia in sote posit tabernaculum suum, et ipse tanquam sponsus proceedens de thalamo suo, exsultavit ut seguirs ai currendam viam'. lile ante solem qui fecit solem, ille ante luciferum, ante omnia sidera, ante omnes Angelos, verus creator (quia omnia per ipsum facta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil \ ut videretur oculis carneis qui solem vident; ipsum tabernaculum suum in solé posit, id est carnem suam in manifestatione huius lucis ostendit: et illius sponsi thalamus Fuit uterus Virginis, quia in illo uterus virginali coniuncti sunt duo, sponsus et sponsa, sponsus Verbum et sponsa caro; Et erunt duo in carne unas; loquitur enim ex persona Christi, et dicit, Sicut sponso imposuit mihi mitram, et sicut sponsam ornavit me ornamento 7. 3. He said: We are witnesses and announce to you eternal life, which was in the Father and was manifested in us, that is, it was manifested among us. This could be said more clearly: it was manifested to us. What we saw and heard we announce to you. Pay attention to your charity: We announce to you the things that we saw and heard. They saw the Lord present in the flesh and heard the words of his mouth and announced them to us; We also heard them, but we did not see him. Are we then less happy than them, who saw and heard him? So how does he add so that you also have communion with us? They saw him, we did not see him, and yet we are their partners, because we have the same faith. One, seeing, did not believe, and desired to touch him in order to believe. He said: I will by no means believe unless I put my fingers into the place of his nails and feel his scars. Christ, certainly, temporarily offered himself to be touched by the hands of men, who continually offers himself to be contemplated by the gaze of angels. That disciple, then, touched him and exclaimed: My Lord and my God; Touching the man, he confessed God. But the Lord, to console those of us who cannot, because we are already seated in heaven, touch him with our hands, but with faith, said to the disciple: Because you saw me, you believed; blessed are those who do not see and believe. In these we are represented, we are designated. May the happiness that the Lord predicted as future take place in us. Let us hold firmly to what we do not see, because it is announced to us by those who saw. This is how that will apply to us: So that you also may have partnership with us. And what is the value of having a society with men? Don't despise her; attend to what 3. Et testes, inquit, sumus; et annuntiamus vobis vitam aeternam, quae erat apud Patrem, et manifestata est in nobis: hoc est, manifestata est. inter nos; quod apertius diceretur, manifestata est nobis. Quae ergo vidimus et atidivimas, nuntiamus vobis. Intendat Charitas vestra: Quae ergo vidimus et audivimus, nuntiamus vobis. lili viderunt ipsum Dominum praesentem in carne, et audierunt verba ex ore Domini, et annuntiaverunt nobis. Et nos ergo audimus, sed non vidimus. Minus ergo sumus Feliz quam illi qui viderunt et audierunt? Et quomodo adiungit: Ut et vos societatem habeatis nobiscum? lili viderunt, nos non vidimus, et taraen socii sumus: quia fidem communem tenemus.

Nam et quídam videndo non credidit, et palpare voluit, et sic credere, et ait: Non credam nisi digits meos misero in locum clavarum, et scars eius tetigero. Et praebuit se ex tempore palpandum manibus hominum, qui always se praebet videndum aspectibus Angelorum: et palpayit Ule discipulus et exclamavit, Dominas meus et Deus meus. Quia tetigit hominem, confessus est Deum. Et Dominus consolans nos qui ipsum iam in cáelo sedentem manu contrectare non possumus, sed fide contingere, ait illi: Quia vidisti, ciedidisti; beati qui non vident et credunt". Nos descripti sumus. nos designati sumus. Fiat ergo in nobis beatitudo quam Dominus praedixitfuturam: firma teneamus quod non videmus; quia illi nuntiant qui viderunt. Ut et vos, inquit, societatem habeatis nobiscum. Et quid magnum

adds: And our society will be with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ. We write this to you so that your joy may be complete. He calls full joy what there is in this society, in this charity, in this unity. 4. And this is the message that we heard from Him, and that we communicate to you. Which is it? They saw and touched with their hands the Word of life; from the beginning he existed, but the only begotten Son of God became visible and palpable in time. What did he come for? What new thing did he announce? What did you want to teach? What purpose did he have in doing what he did, that is, becoming the Word flesh; to suffer God, who is above all things, insults from men; endure the slaps of those whose hands he himself formed? What did he want to teach, what did he want to demonstrate, what to announce? Let us listen, because the mere hearing of past events: that Christ was born and suffered, without the fruit of instruction, is entertainment for the mind, but not sustenance for it. What good is mere hearing to you? Pay attention to the profit with which you hear. What did you want to teach? What to announce? Listen: God is light and in Him there is no trace of darkness. Here he has certainly named the light, but the words are dark; It is convenient for us that the same light that he named illuminates our hearts to understand what he said. What we announce to you is this: that God is light and in Him there is no trace of darkness. Who will dare to say that there is darkness in God? What is this light, what is the darkness? Lest I speak of the things that belong to these our carnal eyes. God, he says, is light. Someone will say: The sun is also light, the moon is light, and likewise a lamp is light. It must be something much greater than these lights, more powerful, much more excellent. How much God differs from the creature, how much societatem habere cum hominibus? Noli contemnere; vide quid addat: Et societas nostra sit cum Deo Patre, et lesu Christo Filio eius. Et haec, inquit, scribimus vobis, ut gaudium vestrum sit plenum. Plenum gaudium dicit in ipsa societate, in ipsa charitate, in ipsa unitate. 4. Et haec est annuntiatio quam audivimus ab eo, et annuntiamus vobis. Quid est hoc? Ipsi viderunt, contrectaverunt manibus Verbum vitae: ab initio erat, ad tempus visibilis et palpabilis factus est unicus Filius Dei. Ad quam rem venit, vel quid nobis novum nuntiavit? Quid docere voluit? Quare fecit hoc quod fecit, ut Verbum caro ieront, ut Deus super omnia indigna ab hominibus pateretur, ut alapas eorum sustineret de manibus quas ipse formavit?

Quid voluit docere? quid voluit otendere? quid voluit annuntiare? Audiamus: nam sine fructu praecepti, auditorio rei gestae, quia natus est Christus, et quia passus est Christus, avocamentum mentís est, non firmamentum. Quid magnum audis? quo fructu audis, vide. Quid voluit docere? What will I announce? Audi: Quia Deus lux est, inquit, et tenebrae in eo non sunt ullae. Adhuc luzem quidem nominavit, sed obscura sunt verba: bonum est nobis ut ipsa lux quam nominavit, illustret corda nostra, et videamus quid dixit. Hoc est quod annuntiamus, quia Deus lux est, et tenebrae in eo non sunt ullae. Quis enim auderet dicere quia in Deo sunt tenebrae? Aut quid est ipsa lux? aut quid sunt tenebrae? ne forte talia dicat, quae ad oculos istos nostros pertineant. Deus lux est:

The Creator is distant from creation, as Wisdom distances itself from that which was made by it, so must this light transcend all things. But perhaps we will be close to it if we know what this light is and we approach it so that it illuminates us. We are darkness, but we can be light illuminated by it, without being confused because of it, because the confusion comes from us. Who is confused about himself? He who recognizes himself as a sinner. Who is not confused because of that light? The one who is illuminated by it. What is it to be enlightened by it? Seeing yourself darkened by sins, and, desiring to be illuminated by it, approach it. This is why the psalm says: Draw near to Him and you will be enlightened, and your faces will not be ashamed. You will not be ashamed of her if, when she shows you deformed, you dislike your ugliness in order to perceive her beauty. This is what he wants to teach. 5. Perhaps we have said this too early? He demonstrates it in what follows. Remember that at the beginning of our exposition I said that this Epistle recommends charity: God, it says, is light and in Him there is no trace of darkness. What had he said before? So that you may have communion with us and our communion may be with God the Father and his Son Jesus Christ. Therefore, if God is light and there is no trace of darkness in Him, and we must form a partnership with Him, and the darkness must be cast out of us so that the light may enter into us, because the darkness cannot be combined with the light, pay attention, for the same reason, to what follows: If we said that we form soait nescio quis, Et sol lux est, et luna lux est, et luzern lux est. Aliquid debent esse longe his maius, longe praestantius, longeque supereminentius. Quantum Deus a creature, quantum conditor a conditione, quantum sapientia ab eo quod factum est per sapientiam, longe ultra omnia debent esse lux ista. Et forte vicini ei erimus, si quae sit lux ista cognoverimus, et ad eam nos applicavetimus, ut ex ipsa illuminemur; quia in nobis tenebrae sumus, ct ab illa ¡Iluminad possumus esse lux, et non confundí de illa, quia de nobis confundimur. Quis est qui de se confunditur? Qui se eognoscit peccatorem. Quis de illa non confunditur? Qui ab illa illuminatur. What is the illuminari? Qui iam videt se peccatis tenebrari, et cupit ab illa illuminari, accessit ad illam: unde dicit Psalmps, Accedite ad eum, et illuminamini; et vultus vestri non erubescent °.

Sed non erubesces de illa, si, quando tibi te foeduní ostenderit, displiceat tibi foeditas tua, ut percipias pulchritudinem illius. Hoc est quod vult docere. 5. Et fortasse praepropere illud nos dicimus? Ipse hoe manifestet in consequentibus. Mementote in principle sermonis nostri, quia Epístola ista charitatem commendaf. Deus lux est, inquit, et tenebrae in eo non sunt ullae. Et quid superius dixerat? Ut societatem habeatis nobiscum, et societas nostra sit cum Deo Paire et Filio eius lesu Christo. Porro si Deus lux est, et tenebrae in eo non sunt ullae, et societatem cum illo habere debenmus; et a nobis pellendae sunt tenebrae, ut fiat in nobis lux; nam tenebrae cum luz societatem habere non possunt; ideo vide quid sequatur: Quod si dixerimus quia societatem, habemus cum eo, et in teñe « P s. 33.6.

fellowship with Him and we walk in darkness, we lie. The apostle Saint Paul tells you the same thing: What communion is there between light and darkness? Let the man say: What shall I do? How will I be light? I live in evil and sins. A certain despair and sadness has taken over him. There is no salvation except in communion with God. God is light and there is no trace of darkness in Him. Sins are darkness, for the Apostle says: The devil and his angels are the rulers of this darkness. I would not say that they are the rulers of darkness, unless they are the rulers of sins, the dominators of the wicked. What shall we do, brothers? Communion with God is imposed; Otherwise there is no hope of eternal life. God is light and in Him there is no trace of darkness. Iniquities are darkness; They force us to not be able to have communion with God; So what hope do we have? But didn't I promise that I would talk these days about something that would cause joy? If I now offer the opposite, what I cause is sadness. God is light and in Him there is no trace of darkness. Darkness are the sins. What will become of us? Let's listen: it will undoubtedly console us, give us encouragement and hope so as not to faint along the way. We run, we run towards the homeland; but, if we despair of arriving, we faint through the same despair. He, who wants us to reach it, feeds us along the way so that we arrive safely at home. Let us hear, then: If we say that we have communion with Him and we walk in darkness, we lie and do not act the truth. Let's not say that bris ambulamus, mentimur. Habes et apostolum Paulum dicentem. Iam ergo dicat sibi homo. Quid faciam? where was lux? In peccatis et in iniquitatibus vivo. Quasi subrepit quaedam desperation et tristitia. Salus nulla est. nisi in societate Dei. Societas cum Deo habenda est, alia spes vitae aeternae nulla est; Deus autem lux est, et tenebrae in eo sunt nullae: iniquitates autem tenebrae sunt: iniquitatibus premimur, ne societatem cum Deo habere possimus: quae ergo spes? Nonne promiseram me aliquid locuturum istis diebus quod gaudium faciat? What if I don't exhibit? tristitia est ist. Currimus enim, et ad patriam currimus; et si nos perventuros deesperamus, ipsa desperatione deficimus. lile autem qui nos vult parvenire, ut conservet in patria, pascit in via. With Him we have society if we walk in darkness.' But, if we walk in the light, just as He is in the light, there will be communion between Him and us. Let us walk in the light as He is in the light, so that with Him we may have fellowship. And what will we do about our sins? Listen to what follows: And the blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, will cleanse us from all crime. God gave great security. On this occasion we celebrate Easter, in which the blood of Christ was shed, with which we purified ourselves from all sin. Let's be sure; The devil had the deed of bondage against us, but by the blood of Christ it was destroyed. The blood of Christ, his Son, will cleanse us from all sin. What does it mean about every crime or sin? Pay attention, see that in the name of Christ, by his blood, to whom these who are called infants now confess, all their sins have been erased. Old people came in, new people came out. What does it mean, old people came in, new people came out? Elders entered, infants left. Decrepit old age is ancient life; regenerated childhood is new life. And we, what will we do? Past sins have been forgiven, not only for them, but for us as well. But after the forgiveness and abolition of all sins, by living in this world among temptations, perhaps some others have been contracted. Therefore, let man do what he can, confess what he is, so that he may be healed by Him who always is what he is. He always was and is; we were not and we are.

6. Pay attention to what it says: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. Therefore, if you confess yourself a sinner, the truth is in you: the truth is light. Even your life does not shine in all its brilliance, because there are sins in you; but you are already beginning to be enlightened, since you confess your iniquities. Look at what follows: If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity. Not only the past ones, but also those that we have contracted in the current life, since man, during the time he carries his flesh, cannot help but have sins, even if they are only slight. But let us not despise these things that we call mild. If you don't get scared when we weigh them, be horrified when you count them. Many small things make one great thing; many drops form a river; many grains make an immense collection. And what hope is left? First of all, confession, no one believing himself to be righteous, nor raising his neck the man who was not and is, in the sight of God, who sees what he is. First, the confession; then, love. What was said about charity? Charity covers the multitude of sins. Let us now see how he recommends the same charity due to the crimes that enter man as if by stealth, since only it erases sins. Pride extinguishes charity; humility strengthens love; Charity erases sins. Humility concerns confession, by which we recognize ourselves as sinners. This is humility; not to confess it only with the tongue moved by a kind of pride, in order not to displease men, saying that we are just. The wicked and

latera habemus cum eo, et in tenebris ambulamus, mentimur, et non facimus veritatem. Non dicamus quia societatem cum illo habemus. if in tenebris ambulamus. Quod si in lamine ambulamus, sicut et ipse est in lumine; societatem habemus cum invicem. In lumine ambulemus, sicut et ipse est in lumine, ut possimus societatem habere cum illo. Et quid facimus de peccatis? Audi quid sequitur: Et sanguis lesu Christi Füii eius purgabit nos ab omni delicio. Magnam securitatem dedit Deus. Merit Pascha celebramus, ubi fusus est sanguis Domini, quo purgamur ab omni delicto. Simus securi: cautionem contra nos servitutis diabolus tenebat, sed sanguine Christi deleta est. Sanguis, inquit, Filii eius purgabit nos ab omni delicio. Quid est, ab omni delicto? Attendite: ecce iam in nomine Christi per sanguinem eius, quem nunc confessi sunt isti qui appellantur infantes, mundata sunt omnia peccata ipsorum. Veteres intraverunt, novi exierunt. Quid est, veteres intraverunt, novi exierunt? Senes intraverunt, infantes exierunt. Senectus enim veternosa, vetusta vita: infantia autem regenerationis, nova vita. Sed quid facimus? Praeterita peccata donata sunt', non tantum ipsis, sed et nobis; et post donationem et abolitionem omnium peccatorum vivir in hoc saeculo inter temptationes, quaedam forte contracta sunt. Ideo quod potest homo facial; ipse confiteatur quod est, ut ab illo curetur qui semper est quod est: ipse enim semper erat et est; nos non eramus et sumus.

Ergo si te confessus fueris peccatorem, est in te veritas: nam ipsa veritas lux est. Nondum perfecte splenduit vita tua, quia insunt peccata; sed tamen iam Illuminate coepisti, quia inest confessio peccatorum. Vide enim quid sequatur: Quod si confessi fuerimus delicia nostra, jidelis est et iustus, ut dimittat nobis delicia nostra, et purgel nos ex omni iniquitate. Non tantum praeterita, sed et si qua forte contraximus ex hac vita; Quia non potest homo quamdiu carnem portat, nisi hare vel levia peccata. Sed is ista levia quae dicimus, noli contemnere. Si contemnis, quando appendis; expavesce, when you number. Levia Fine Faciunt Unum Grande: Multac Guttae Implent Flumen; fine grana faciunt massam. Et quae spes est? Ante omnia confessio: ne quisquam se iustum putet, et ante oculos Dei qui videt quod est, erigat cervicem homo qui non erat et est. Ante omnia ergo confessio, deinde dilectio: quia de charitate quid dictum est? Charilas cooperit multitudinem peccatorum 12. Iam videamus si ipsam charitatem commendat, Jjropter subrepentia delicta: quia sola charitas exstinguit delicta. Humilitas pertinet ad confessionem, qua confitemur nos peccatores esse: ipsa est humilitas, non ut dicamus illud lingua; quasi propter arrogantiam ne displiceamus hominibus, si nos iustos esse dixe12

wicked people proceed in this way: I know, they say, certainly that I am righteous; But how should I say it to men? If I say that I am just, who will put up with me, who will tolerate me? Only my justice remains for God. For my part, I will say that I am a sinner, not because I am, but so as not to make myself hateful for my presumption. Tell men what you are, tell it to God, because, if you do not tell God what you are, God will condemn what he finds in you. Don't you want Him to condemn you? Condemn yourself. Do you want Him to forgive you? Recognize yourself so that you can say to him: Turn your attention away from my sins. Also tell him the words of the same psalm: I recognize my iniquities. If we confess our crimes, it is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity. If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is absent from us. If you say: I have not sinned, you make God a liar by wanting to make you truthful. How can it happen that God is a liar and man is truthful, contradicting the Scripture, which states: Every man is a liar; God alone is truthful? Therefore God by himself is true; you for God's sake, since on your part you are mendacious. 7. And lest perhaps he may seem to have granted impunity to sin by saying: He is faithful and just to forgive us all sin, and, therefore, it may be said to men: Let us sin, let us do safely what we want, since Christ purifies us, he is faithful and just and cleanses us from all sin, the apostle removes this disastrous assurance from you and instills a deep fear in your heart. Faciunt hoc impii et insani: Scio quidem quia iustus sum, sed quid dicturus sum ante homines? si me iustum dixero, quis ferat, quis toleret? apud Deum Nota sit iustitia mea: ego tamen dicam me peccatorem; Non quia sum, sed ne arrogance odiosus inveniar. Dic hominibus quod es, dic Deo quod es. Quia si non dixeris Deo quod es, damnat Deus quod in te inveniet.

It is certain whether this life is useful or useless to anyone, but life in God is, without a doubt, useful to all. Love your enemies in such a way that you consider them brothers. In these justice is perfect; in us it is in its beginnings, born of faith according to the Spirit. You heard when reading the psalm: Begin by confessing the Lord. Begin, he says. Everyone who commits sin perpetrates iniquity, since sin is iniquity. What will we do about our sins and iniquities? Hear what he says: And you know that He appeared to take away sin, and in Him there is no sin. He in whom there is no sin came to take away sin. If there were sin in Him, it should be taken away from Him, not taken away by Him. Whoever abides in Him does not sin. As long as he does not sin, as long as he remains in Him. Everyone who sins has neither seen Him nor known Him. This is a great question. Everyone who sins has neither seen nor known Him. No wonder. We have not yet seen him, but we must see him; we have not known him, but we must know him; We believe in him whom we do not know. Or is it that perhaps we know him by faith and we do not yet know him by vision? By faith we have seen and known him. If faith does not yet see him, why do we call ourselves enlightened? Our righteousness will be perfect when we contemplate by vision. Now let us not abandon justice, which comes from faith, because the righteous live by faith, as the Apostle says. Whoever abides in Him does not sin. For everyone who sins has neither seen him nor known him. He who sins does not believe, because if he believes, he does not sin as much as it depends on his faith. 8. Omnis qui facit peccatum, et iniquitatem facit. Nemo dicat, Aliud est peccatum, aliud iniquitas: nemo dicat, Ego peccator homo sum, sed iniquus non sum. Omnis enim qui facit peccatum, et iniquitatem facit. Peccatum est iniquitas. Quid ergo facimus of peccatis nostris et iniquitatibus? Audi quid dicat: Et scitis quia ille manifestatus est, ut peccatum auferat; et peccatum in ipso non est. In quo non est peccatum, ipse venit auferre peccatum. Nam si esset et in illo peccatum, auferendum esset illi, non ipse auferret. Omnis qui in ipso manet, non peccat. In quantum in ipso manet, in tantum non peccat. Omnis qui peccat, non vidit eum, ñeque cognovit eum. Magna ista quaestio: Omnis qui peccat, non vidit eum, ñeque cognovit eum. Non est mirum. 9. Little children, let no one deceive you. He who works righteousness is righteous, just as He is righteous. Should we, when we hear that we are righteous like Him, judge ourselves equal to God? You must know what sicut (like) means. He already said before: He purifies Himself AS He is pure. Is our purity then identical with the purity of God, and our justice with the justice of God? Who will say this? The word sicut (as) does not always compare and equal. For example: If someone, seeing this large basilica, would like to make a smaller one, but, nevertheless, keeping the proportions in his measurements, so that, if it is twice as long as it is wide, he also makes the one he intends to be twice as long as it is wide, it will be said that he made it like (sicut), but in a smaller proportion. But this one measures, for example, a hundred cubits; that one, thirty; Therefore, it is like this and it is unequal. You saw that the word sicut does not always denote parity and equality. See how much difference there is between the man's face and his image in the mirror. There is a face in the image, there is a face in the body; the image is an imitation; the body, a reality. And yet, what do we say? As the eyes are here, they are also there; As there are ears here, there are also ears there; Unequal is reality, but the word like (sicut) says similarity.
